title: How Long Does Postpartum Psychosis Last? Recovery and Long-Term Outlook
summary: How long does postpartum psychosis last? Learn the typical timeline with treatment, what recovery looks like, whether it can come back, and the long-term outlook.
body_markdown:
## Postpartum Psychosis Recovery


Recovery from postpartum psychosis unfolds in stages rather than a single moment. The acute phase is about safety and stabilization, usually in a hospital. The same treatment study found that a structured, stepwise approach, using benzodiazepines to restore sleep, then antipsychotic medication, then[lithium](https://lifestance.com/psychiatric-medication/lithium-carbonate-lithobid-eskalith/) , brought 98.4% of women to full remission, with none requiring electroconvulsive therapy, the last treatment option.


Sustained remission at nine months was achieved in roughly four of five patients, and women maintained on lithium relapsed significantly less often than those on antipsychotic medication alone. Which medication a clinician chooses depends on the individual situation: the diagnosis behind the symptoms, prior response to treatment, whether the mother is breastfeeding, and which side effects matter most to her. As with all psychiatric care, medications are prescribed only when a clinician judges them appropriate and should be taken only as directed.


After the acute phase has passed, what comes next is rebuilding sleep, gradually resuming care of the baby, processing what happened, and continuing[medication management](https://lifestance.com/psychiatric-medication/) with a[psychiatrist](https://lifestance.com/provider/psychiatrist/) as symptoms stay quiet.


It is very important to stop medication safely. A doctor should decide when and how to slowly lower the dose. Many women taking an antipsychotic prescription fully recover and can reduce their medication over time with medical guidance. Stopping medication on your own, even when you feel better, can slow or interrupt recovery.


Many women also struggle with difficult feelings afterward. They may grieve the early months they missed with their baby and family, worry about being judged, or have painful memories of the illness or hospital stay. Once the acute illness has ended, therapy can be a helpful part of recovery. It gives a mother a place to talk about what happened and how she feels about it. Many types of therapy can help, from[one-on-one talk therapy](https://lifestance.com/services/talk-therapy/) to approaches[designed for trauma](https://lifestance.com/services/trauma-informed-care/) .[Group therapy](https://lifestance.com/services/group-therapy/) can also help, since connecting with other mothers who have been through a postpartum mental health crisis is a reminder that no one goes through this alone.
